title: the prayer you know by heart
hook: a king who tried to take by force, and the prayer he's remembered for: asking only for a clear mind
carry: a prayer for a clear mind

segments.voice: Yesterday: om, three sounds and a silence. Today it opens a prayer you might already know by heart.

Om bhur bhuvah svah. If you grew up in a Hindu home, there's a good chance you can say the rest without thinking. Maybe someone said it every morning. Maybe it played at every puja. Now the hard part: what does it ask for? Most people go quiet. The answer starts with a king who wanted something he couldn't take. First, a guess.
screen: `OM BHUR BHUVAH SVAH…` → `YOU CAN SAY IT.` → `WHAT DOES IT ASK FOR?`

segments.voice: Long ago a powerful king, Vishvamitra, stopped with his army at the forest home of the sage Vasishtha. The sage fed every soldier, thanks to a wondrous cow that could give anything. The king wanted her. He offered herds of cattle, gold, jewels. The sage said no. So the king tried to take her by force, and lost: his armies and his weapons failed against one sage with a staff. Stung, he gave up his throne and spent years in practice, failing and starting over, until at last even Vasishtha honored him as a great sage. Tradition names Vishvamitra as the seer of the prayer many Hindus say at dawn: the Gayatri. Listen to what it asks. Bhur bhuvah svah: earth, sky, and beyond. Tat savitur varenyam: that worthy light of Savitar, the sun that stirs the world awake. Bhargo devasya dhimahi: we meditate on that divine radiance. Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat: may it wake up and guide our minds. Not a cow. Not a kingdom. Not to win. A clear mind. The man who tried to take everything by force is remembered for a prayer that asks only to see. That's a mantra: man, to think, and tra, a tool. Some traditions teach the Gayatri at a coming-of-age ceremony; in many homes, everyone simply says it. If you grew up saying it without the meaning, you weren't doing it wrong. The night before an exam or a hard talk, it doesn't ask for the result. It asks for a mind that sees straight.
screen: `A KING WHO TRIED FORCE.` · `YEARS OF PRACTICE. THE GAYATRI.` · `MAY IT WAKE UP OUR MINDS.` · `MANTRA — A TOOL FOR THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Breathe in. As you breathe out, say the Gayatri once, slowly, out loud or in your head, or just its last line: dhiyo yo nah prachodayat, may it wake up and guide our minds. This time, mean the words.
Gayatri. The morning prayer for a clear mind, and a mantra: a tool for the mind. Third word on your strand.
Your line: a prayer for a clear mind. Next time you hear it, you'll know what's being asked. Day three.

story.title: the king who wanted to be a sage
story.text: A powerful king named Vishvamitra tried to take a holy cow from a sage by force, and lost, badly, to a man with no army at all. Stung, he gave up his kingdom and spent years in practice, failing and starting again, until even the sage he'd fought called him a great sage. Tradition says he's the one who first heard the Gayatri.
story.source: the Ramayana's telling of Vishvamitra (Bala Kanda); tradition names him the Gayatri's seer
